fields.meta_title: Travel Landing Page Builder for Tour Operators | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build a travel landing page from a prompt. See four examples: tour seats by date, trip requests by country, a retreat vote, and a room block.
fields.h1: Build a Travel Landing Page for Tours, Retreats, and Group Trips
fields.hero_description: Get a travel landing page that takes trip requests, sends each to the right advisor and saves it to a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What Happens After a Traveler Hits Send
fields.features_subheading: Emergent builds the page a traveler reads and the logic that handles each request once it arrives.
fields.feature_1:
Describe the trip, get the page

Write the itinerary and the form you need in plain English, and Emergent builds the page along with the table that stores each request. A new departure date is one more prompt.
fields.feature_2:
Requests in a table you own

Each request is saved to a database you own, with the trip, the travel month, and the party size in their own columns. Sort by month to see which season visitors ask about.
fields.feature_3:
Seat limits per date

Give each departure its seat limit in the prompt. The app subtracts every reservation from that date, shows travelers what remains, and offers a waitlist once it is full.
fields.feature_4:
The right advisor hears first

Name who answers which trips, such as one advisor for each country you sell. The app sends that person an email or a Slack alert with the traveler's details and the dates requested.
fields.feature_5:
Requests that reach your booking tools

The app connects to any tool with an API, so a new request can sync to your CRM or your email platform. Data moves in and out, and your own table keeps the original entry.
fields.feature_6:
Your domain, and the code if you want it

Publish on your own domain: custom domains are included and use credits. On paid plans, export the full code to your GitHub repository and keep building on it from there.

fields.tab_content_1:
Seats left show next to each departure

Larchmoor Expeditions sells its 8-day Iceland ring-road tour in groups of 12. The page lists three departures with the seats left beside each one: June 27 has 3 and July 18 has 8. June 6 is full: its button now reads Join the waitlist, and 5 travelers have joined it.
fields.tab_content_2:
Any request for Japan goes to Keiko Arakawa

Marisco Travel's trip request form asks for the country, the month, and the number of travelers. The app emails each request to the advisor for that country: Japan to Keiko Arakawa, Italy to Matteo Bellandi. Ines Paredes asked for Kyoto in April for 5 travelers, and the email went to Keiko.
fields.tab_content_3:
November drew the most votes, so it opens first

Before Amberwood Retreats fixes next year's dates for its Costa Rica yoga retreat, its page asks visitors which month suits them. Of 73 answers, 41 chose November, 20 chose January, and 12 chose March. November opens first, and on the day reservations open, the app emails all 41 people who picked it.
fields.tab_content_4:
At midnight on March 15 the room block closes

Coralline Group Travel holds 30 rooms at a beach resort for the Sorensen-Ruiz wedding, and guests claim theirs on a room block page. So far 22 are claimed and 8 are left. Every Monday, planner Yolanda Ferreira gets an email with both counts. The form closes at midnight on March 15, the resort's release date.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Travel Landing Page
fields.howto_description: Follow these seven steps to publish a travel landing page that takes requests for one trip and sends each to the right person.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Give each trip its own page
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Lead with the dates and the price
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Write the trip into one prompt
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Set the limits before you share it
fields.howto_step_1_des: Build one page per trip. A traveler who clicked an ad for an Iceland tour should land on that tour's dates and price, not on a list of every departure you run this year.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Put the next departure dates and the price per person at the top, with the group size beside them. Those are the details a traveler compares before typing an email address.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Tell Emergent the form fields you need and what should happen after a request arrives. Emergent builds the page and its table, and a later prompt changes either one.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Write the seat count for each departure, or the room count and cutoff date for a block, into the prompt. Then decide what a visitor sees at the limit: a waitlist, or a note naming the next date.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Match each request to a person
fields.howto_step_5_des: Decide who answers which requests and name them in the prompt. A request someone should read the same day gets an instant email; a weekly count suits a planner who tracks a room block.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Book a test seat from a phone
fields.howto_step_6_des: Open the published page on a phone and send a request with your own email. Check that the row reached the table and the email reached the right advisor, then fill a test departure and watch the waitlist open.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Put the link where travelers plan
fields.howto_step_7_des: Share the page in your newsletter and in the emails past travelers already open. Each week, check which pages drew requests and rework the ones that drew none.

faq_plan.q: What is a travel landing page?
faq_plan.a: A travel landing page is a single web page built around one trip, such as a guided tour or a yoga retreat, that asks the visitor to send one request. It shows the dates and the price, then a single form, without the menus of a full travel website.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a travel landing page?
faq_plan.a: Describe the trip in a prompt, with its dates and the questions the form should ask, and Emergent's AI landing page builder builds the page and the database behind the form. Publish it on your own domain, then send yourself a test request from a phone before you share the link.

faq_plan.q: Are travel landing page templates worth starting from?
faq_plan.a: They are worth it for layout ideas, less so for what happens after a request. A template hands you a photo header and a form, but the layout alone does not decide who answers each request or what a full departure shows. Keep the layout you like, then describe the request flow in your own prompt.

faq_plan.q: Should each tour get its own travel landing page?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Each tour has its own dates and seat count, and an ad for one trip should land on that trip. When you sell several trips in one region, add a category landing page that lists them and links to each trip's page.

faq_plan.q: What should a travel landing page show above the fold?
faq_plan.a: The trip name, its length, the next dates, and what one traveler pays, next to the button to request a spot. Show those four details before anything else. Move the day-by-day itinerary and the guide bios further down the page.

faq_plan.q: How do I keep large destination photos from slowing down my travel landing page?
faq_plan.a: Compress the header photo, serve it at the size it displays, and measure the page before you share it. Google's web.dev guide sets the target. "To provide a good user experience, sites should strive to have Largest Contentful Paint of 2.5 seconds or less." Check which element the measurement names, and when it is a full-width photo, shrink that photo first.

faq_plan.q: Can a tour company use a travel landing page to hire seasonal guides?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Give the hiring season its own page with the role and season dates above a short application form, the same pattern recruiting landing pages follow. Keep it apart from your trip pages. Applicants and travelers then each find one form meant for them.

faq_plan.q: How many fields should the form on a travel landing page have?
faq_plan.a: Four is enough for the first reply: a name, an email, the month they want to travel, and the group size. Dietary needs and room preferences can wait for the follow-up call. The app Emergent builds saves each request to a database you own, and the advisor can add those details to the same record later.

faq_plan.q: Can requests from a travel landing page go into the CRM my agency already uses?
faq_plan.a: Yes, when that CRM has an API. The app Emergent builds can connect to it and sync each new request in. Advisors keep working in the tool they know, and the original entry stays in your own table. Ask your CRM provider which records its API accepts before you plan the sync.

faq_plan.q: Can a travel landing page for one group trip grow into a small site?
faq_plan.a: Yes. When a trip needs more than one page, such as an itinerary and a packing list, a microsite landing page keeps them together under one address. Start with the request page, then prompt Emergent to add the other pages as the trip fills.

plan.angle: The results for this keyword are design galleries, vector stores and example roundups that show how a travel page looks, never what happens to a booking request once it is sent. This page shows four travel landing pages a tour operator, an agency, a retreat host and a group travel planner build from a prompt, and follows each request to where it goes: seats left per departure with a waitlist on a full date, trip requests routed to the advisor who covers the country, a retreat interest page whose vote picks next year's month, and a wedding room block that closes on the resort's release date. The FAQ covers the definition, building one, what to take from templates, one page per trip, what goes first, photo weight, hiring guides, form length, agency software and a small site for one trip.
